theme_scores.justification: The claim is supported by cited Scottish findings ('the number of letting agents in Scotland has increased since the ban indicating that the sector has become more competitive' and '56% of private tenants agreed... improves the rental sector', Reference 16) plus an uncited assertion that 'there is evidence that a number of agents are charging excessive fees and that some agents are double charging landlords and tenants', reaching level 2 via the cited Scottish link but not assessed with uncertainty specifically on this mechanism.
These lines only describe what the ban will cover (fees, premiums, charges) with no evidence offered for why this particular scope was chosen.

The theme cites a named, linked report (Reference 16, Shelter/Rettie/BDRC Continental) with specific figures (17% of agencies increased fees, 56% tenant agreement, number of agents up) and explicitly flags its own uncertainty ('this is inconclusive', 'It is difficult to directly compare the English and Scottish markets').

theme_scores.theme: Expected rent effects and net benefit
theme_scores.justification: The claim of partial pass-through is grounded in the cited Scottish evidence ('agents, in order to remain competitive, are unlikely to pass the full costs of the fees onto landlords', Reference 16) immediately qualified by the acknowledged limitation that English and Scottish markets are hard to compare directly.

reasoning: The core argument rests on four themes. 'Scope of the ban' (level 0) simply describes what will be banned with no supporting evidence. 'Rebalancing market power' (level 2) draws on the cited Scottish data showing agent numbers rising and tenant approval (56%), linked via Reference 16, though the specific competition mechanism isn't separately assessed for uncertainty. 'Scottish precedent' (level 3) is the strongest: it names and links a specific report (Reference 16, Shelter/Rettie/BDRC) with figures, and explicitly weighs contradictory findings ('this is inconclusive', 'difficult to directly compare the English and Scottish markets'). 'Expected rent effects' (level 3) inherits this same cited, uncertainty-qualified Scottish evidence ('agents...are unlikely to pass the full costs of the fees onto landlords'). The mean of (2+0+3+3)/4 = 2.0, giving a section score of 2. The strongest counter-example is 'Scope of the ban', which has essentially no evidential backing at all, showing the evidence base is uneven across the core themes. To reach level 3 overall, the document would need to similarly cite and critically assess evidence for why the ban's precise scope (covering landlords and third parties, not just agents) was chosen, rather than relying solely on the Scottish comparison for the market-power and rent-effect claims.
